Covering rare outcomes in imbalanced regression with conformal prediction: guarantees, size-optimal scores and what tail coverage costs

[Anonymised for double-blind review: author names and affiliations are given on the separate title page]

Abstract

Conformal prediction intervals are usually calibrated on average over all outcomes, so they can miss the rare, extreme outcomes that matter most in imbalanced regression. Even an ideal interval with exact coverage at every input covers only 70.5% of the top decile in a Gaussian model with half of the variance explained. We study how to guarantee coverage of rare outcomes and what it costs. On 31 datasets of the OpenML-CTR23 benchmark suite, standard conformal methods covered only 63.0%–78.3% of their worst-covered target stratum at a nominal 90%. Calibrating within target strata restored coverage in every stratum and enlarged sets by a factor of about 1.24, less than lowering the overall miscoverage level would. We show that conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds are the smallest stratum-valid sets. Their plug-in method, stratified density-level conformal prediction (SDLC), gave smaller sets than stratified absolute-residual and quantile methods, as a pre-specified analysis confirmed on 17 held-out datasets, but within a few percent of a stratified normalised residual, which covered the most extreme outcomes better. For coverage weighted by a relevance function, the size-optimal method RW-DLC covered 88.4% of the top 1% of held-out outcomes against 76.0% for SDLC with five strata; dedicated 1% strata matched this coverage but, where sparse, gave sets about a third larger. Both work with any regressor and cost microseconds per prediction in batches. A dedicated stratum suffices for a well-populated extreme range; relevance weighting suits sparse tails and coverage across the whole target range.

Keywords: Conformal prediction; Imbalanced regression; Prediction intervals; Uncertainty quantification; Relevance function; Rare outcomes

1. Introduction

Many regression problems that intelligent systems solve are judged by how they handle rare outcomes: the unusually expensive property, the exceptional salary, the extreme load on a power grid, the very toxic compound. Rare outcomes are under-represented in training data, and models trained by minimising average loss shrink their predictions towards the bulk of the target distribution. This is the setting of imbalanced regression (Branco et al. 2017a; Ribeiro and Moniz 2020; Yang et al. 2021), where a growing literature re-weights, re-samples or re-parameterises models so that point predictions for rare targets become more accurate.

Point predictions are only half of what a decision maker needs. Prediction sets with a coverage guarantee state how far the truth may be from the prediction, and conformal prediction delivers such guarantees in finite samples for any model, under exchangeability only (Vovk et al. 2005; Lei et al. 2018; Angelopoulos and Bates 2023). Its standard guarantee, however, is marginal: the set contains the outcome with probability 1−α1-\alpha on average over all outcomes. When rare outcomes matter, the relevant question is different: when the outcome is extreme, how often does the set contain it? A marginal guarantee is silent on this, because the frequent bulk can be over-covered while the rare tails are under-covered.

Much work makes conformal sets adapt to the covariates, so that coverage holds approximately conditionally on XX (Romano et al. 2019; Chernozhukov et al. 2021; Izbicki et al. 2022; Gibbs et al. 2025). Such sets do not protect rare outcomes, and better estimation would not change this: even the oracle set with exact coverage 1−α1-\alpha at every xx under-covers the tails, because an extreme outcome typically combines a large signal with a large, unpredictable noise realisation that no XX-measurable set can anticipate. Coverage conditional on the target, which we call stratum-wise coverage, must be targeted explicitly.

Calibrating conformal thresholds separately within bins of the observed outcome is the natural device, and it is not new. Randahl et al. (2026) proposed it as bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP) for conflict fatalities, and Wang et al. (2023) calibrate within outcome bins to equalise coverage across groups. Its bin-wise validity is an instance of Mondrian (label-conditional) validity (Vovk et al. 2005; Vovk 2013). Two questions remain open. First, the guarantee holds for any score, so efficiency is decided by the score, and it is not known which score makes stratum-valid sets smallest or what that efficiency costs. Second, strata protect rare outcomes only at their own resolution: the most extreme outcomes lie inside a tail stratum and are covered only on average with it, while finer strata leave too few calibration points. Imbalanced regression usually describes the importance of an outcome by a continuous relevance function (Torgo and Ribeiro 2007; Ribeiro and Moniz 2020; Steininger et al. 2021), and long-tailed classification has obtained conformal guarantees that average coverage over classes (Ding et al. 2025; Bhattacharyya et al. 2026). We address both questions and, above all, what a practitioner should do. Our contributions are four.

  1. Diagnosis. Standard and covariate-adaptive conformal intervals under-cover rare outcomes on almost every dataset, and so does the oracle covariate-conditional interval (Proposition 1: 70.5% of the top decile in a Gaussian model with half of the variance explained), so better models cannot remove the shortfall.
  2. The price of tail validity. Calibrating within target strata restores coverage in every stratum for any score at a size cost of about 1.24, smaller than that of lowering the miscoverage level for all outcomes, and remains exact when the shift re-weights whole strata.
  3. Size-optimal scores for two tail guarantees. Conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds are the smallest stratum-valid sets (Proposition 2, the per-stratum form of known level-set results (Lei et al. 2013; Sadinle et al. 2019)); SDLC is their plug-in method. For relevance-weighted coverage, the average of coverage weighted by a relevance function, relevance-weighted calibration is valid in finite samples (Theorem 2, weighted conformal prediction with known weights) and level sets of relevance times density are size-optimal (Proposition 4); RW-DLC implements them. Its sets resemble those of conformal prediction under an estimated target shift (Yi et al. 2025), and relevance-weighted coverage is a single-weight member of the coverage families of Kandinsky conformal prediction (Bairaktari et al. 2025); what is new is the criterion for imbalanced regression and its evaluation. Empirically, among scores that use the estimated scale the choice changes set sizes by only a few percent, and we report this as a finding.
  4. A decision guide. We compare which guarantee to choose, how to choose strata, sets versus intervals, and set-based alerts versus conformal tail classifiers and conformal selection (Jin and Candès 2023) under explicit costs (Section 7).

Both methods decide coverage exactly at the observed target and compute set geometry on a fine grid, at a cost linear in the number of test points. The evidence comes from all 31 eligible OpenML-CTR23 datasets with 10 predefined splits, where we compare the stratified methods with BCCP, stratified normalised-residual, quantile and HPD scores and seven marginal or covariate-adaptive methods, with ablations of each score component, and from 17 held-out datasets analysed under two pre-specified plans. We also analyse robustness to target shift, imbalance-aware training, a second learner family, and grouped and temporal splits.

Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 formalises the problem, Section 4 presents SDLC and RW-DLC, Sections 5 and 6 describe the experiments and their results, and Sections 7 and 8 discuss them and conclude.

2. Related work

Four lines of work meet in this paper: covariate-adaptive conformal regression, calibration within label-defined categories, imbalanced regression, and conformal prediction under distribution shift.

2.1 Conformal regression and covariate-conditional coverage

Split conformal prediction calibrates a nonconformity score of any fitted regressor on held-out data and guarantees marginal coverage in finite samples under exchangeability (Papadopoulos et al. 2002; Vovk et al. 2005; Lei et al. 2018). Much subsequent work changes the score so that sets adapt to the covariates: normalised residuals (Lei et al. 2018), conformalised quantile regression (CQR) (Romano et al. 2019; Sesia and Candès 2020), distributional conformal prediction (DCP) (Chernozhukov et al. 2021), conformal predictive distributions (Vovk et al. 2019) and jackknife+ (Barber et al. 2021a). A family of methods builds sets from density estimates: conformal density level sets (Lei et al. 2013; Lei and Wasserman 2014), Dist-split and CD-split (Izbicki et al. 2020), HPD-split (Izbicki et al. 2022), conditional histograms (Sesia and Romano 2021), regression-as-classification (Guha et al. 2024) and conformal thresholded intervals (Luo and Zhou 2025). Under coverage constraints indexed by covariate shifts, length-optimal sets are conditional-density level sets with a covariate-dependent level (Kiyani et al. 2024). SDLC uses a score from this family but calibrates it with stratum-specific thresholds.

These methods target approximate covariate-conditional coverage, which cannot be guaranteed in finite samples without further assumptions (Barber et al. 2021b). Relaxations include conditional calibration over classes of covariate groups or shifts (Gibbs et al. 2025), localised calibration (Guan 2023; Hore and Barber 2025), calibration within partitions learned by trees (Cabezas et al. 2025; Santos et al. 2026), and learned scores that reduce conditional miscoverage (Gao et al. 2024; Xie et al. 2024). In intelligent systems, conformal prediction serves as an uncertainty layer, for example for option prices (Bastos 2024), tropical-cyclone tracks (Meng and Song 2024) and uncertainty-aware deep-forest classifiers (Zhang et al. 2025). All these approaches condition, at most, on functions of XX, and Proposition 1 shows that even exact covariate-conditional coverage leaves extreme outcomes under-covered. Covariate-adaptive scores are therefore complementary to stratified calibration, not a substitute.

2.2 Category-, label- and bin-conditional calibration

Mondrian conformal predictors (Vovk et al. 2005, 2022) assign each example to a category that may depend on its label and calibrate within each category, which yields finite-sample category-conditional and, in particular, label-conditional validity (Vovk 2013; Toccaceli and Gammerman 2019; Angelopoulos et al. 2024). In classification, clustered conformal prediction pools classes with similar score distributions (Ding et al. 2023), a device analogous to merging sparse strata. Closest to our optimality result is Sadinle et al. (2019), who showed that the least ambiguous set-valued classifier under class-specific coverage constraints thresholds p(y|x)p(y\,|\, x) at class-specific cut-offs (see also Lei 2014; Chzhen et al. 2021); Proposition 2 is the same characterisation for a continuous outcome. For long-tailed classification, Ding et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2025) interpolate between marginal and class-conditional coverage, and Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) show that label-weighted conformal prediction guarantees macro-coverage and characterise its smallest sets. RW-DLC carries this idea to continuous outcomes, with a relevance function in place of class weights (Section 4.7). Kandinsky conformal prediction (Bairaktari et al. 2025) covers overlapping or fractional groups defined jointly on covariates and labels, with a high-probability guarantee; disjoint target strata are its simplest case, for which Mondrian calibration is exact.

In regression, Mondrian categories have mostly been functions of XX or of the fitted model: binned difficulty estimates (Boström and Johansson 2020), regression trees (Johansson et al. 2018), covariate clusters (Sousa et al. 2024) and quartiles of point predictions (Boruah 2026a), which reports under-coverage of the highest-strength quartile for steel fatigue; worst-bin coverage statistics are biased downwards (Boruah 2026b). Such guarantees do not extend to coverage conditional on YY.

Two regression methods calibrate within bins of the outcome itself. Wang et al. (2023) require coverage to be equal across groups of a sensitive attribute conditionally on the outcome; their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) calibrates within each group and equal-mass outcome bin at bin-specific levels chosen to minimise width, so coverage is equalised across groups but traded across bins. The closest work is BCCP (Randahl et al. 2026), which runs split conformal prediction with a residual score within user-defined outcome bins and returns the union of the per-bin sets or its hull; it guarantees coverage within each bin. Our stratified calibration step (Eqs. 3–4) coincides with BCCP when the absolute-residual score is used, and its validity (Theorem 1) is not claimed as new. BCCP leaves open which score yields the smallest bin-valid sets, where the efficiency comes from, and how the guarantee behaves under label shift; these are the questions we address.

2.3 Imbalanced regression and its uncertainty

Imbalanced regression concerns problems in which the most important targets are rare (Branco et al. 2017a; Ribeiro and Moniz 2020). Utility-based regression encodes their importance through relevance functions (Torgo and Ribeiro 2007), and precision, recall (Torgo and Ribeiro 2009) and SERA (Ribeiro and Moniz 2020) evaluate point predictions on the relevant range. Data-level methods synthesise rare examples, such as SMOTER (Torgo et al. 2013), SMOGN (Branco et al. 2017b) and their successors (Avelino et al. 2024; Belhaouari et al. 2024; Alahyari and Domaratzki 2026; Shahbazi et al. 2026). Algorithm-level methods re-weight the loss, for example DenseWeight (Steininger et al. 2021), label distribution smoothing (Yang et al. 2021) and Balanced MSE (Ren et al. 2022).

Uncertainty has entered this literature mainly as a means to better point predictions: quantile ensembles (Zhu et al. 2026), variational imbalanced regression (Wang and Wang 2023) and UQDIR (Dolar et al. 2025) give no coverage guarantee, and extreme conformal prediction (Pasche et al. 2026) addresses very high confidence levels instead. Guarantees on how often sets contain rare targets have so far come from conflict forecasting and fair regression (Wang et al. 2023; Randahl et al. 2026). For yes/no decisions about extremes, conformal selection (Jin and Candès 2023) and class-conditional conformal tail classifiers exist; we use both as baselines.

2.4 Distribution shift

Weighted conformal prediction handles covariate shift with likelihood-ratio weights (Tibshirani et al. 2019). Under label (target) shift, the law of YY changes while that of XX given YY does not. Re-weighting approaches for classification (Podkopaev and Ramdas 2021) and regression (Yi et al. 2025; Lee et al. 2026) estimate the shift, and exact validity is lost when it is misspecified (Choi 2026). Label-conditional calibration needs no estimate, because a label shift re-weights whole classes (Podkopaev and Ramdas 2021). Stratified calibration carries this property over to regression exactly when the shift re-weights whole strata (Corollary 1), and only approximately otherwise, which our experiments quantify.

3. Preliminaries and problem formulation

3.1 Stratum-wise coverage

Let (X,Y)∈𝒳×ℝ(X,Y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R} have joint law PP, with marginal law PXP_X of the covariates. Table B1 in Appendix B lists the notation. A prediction set is a map CC from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to subsets of ℝ\mathbb{R} whose graph {(x,y):y∈C(x)}\{(x,y):y\in C(x)\} is jointly measurable. Split conformal prediction (Papadopoulos et al. 2002; Lei et al. 2018) guarantees marginal coverage P{Y∈C(X)}≥1−αP\{Y\in C(X)\}\ge 1-\alpha, and much recent work targets approximate covariate-conditional coverage P{Y∈C(X)|X=x}≈1−αP\{Y\in C(X)\,|\, X=x\}\approx 1-\alpha (Romano et al. 2019; Izbicki et al. 2022; Gibbs et al. 2025), which cannot be guaranteed in finite samples without further assumptions (Barber et al. 2021b).

In imbalanced regression the outcomes of interest are rare target values. Let e1<…<eK−1e_1<\dots<e_{K-1} be cut points and B1=(−∞,e1)B_1=(-\infty,e_1), Bk=[ek−1,ek)B_k=[e_{k-1},e_k) for 1<k<K1<k<K, BK=[eK−1,∞)B_K=[e_{K-1},\infty) the resulting target strata, for instance the lower tail, the bulk and the upper tail, with pk=P(Y∈Bk)>0p_k=P(Y\in B_k)>0. It is the regression analogue of class-conditional coverage (Vovk 2013; Sadinle et al. 2019) and the notion behind BCCP (Randahl et al. 2026) and equal opportunity of coverage (Wang et al. 2023). 3.2 Covariate-conditional validity does not imply stratum-wise validity

How large can the shortfall be for the best covariate-conditional set? The simplest model gives an answer.

Proposition 1 (Gaussian model). Let X∼N(0,τ2)X\sim N(0,\tau^2) and Y|X∼N(X,σ2)Y\,|\, X\sim N(X,\sigma^2) with τ2+σ2=1\tau^2+\sigma^2=1 and 0<τ2<10<\tau^2<1, so that R2=τ2R^2=\tau^2 is the fraction of variance explained by the optimal predictor. Let Φ\Phi be the standard normal distribution function, zα=Φ−1(1−α/2)z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2) and Ccov(x)=[x−zασ,x+zασ]C^{\mathrm{cov}}(x)=[x-z_\alpha\sigma,\,x+z_\alpha\sigma], which is, up to Lebesgue-null sets, the unique set of minimal length with P{Y∈C(x)|X=x}≥1−αP\{Y\in C(x)\,|\, X=x\}\ge 1-\alpha for every xx. Then P{Y∈Ccov(X)|Y=y}=Φ(zασ−(1−R2)yτσ)−Φ(−zασ−(1−R2)yτσ),(2)P\{Y\in C^{\mathrm{cov}}(X)\,|\, Y=y\}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{z_\alpha\sigma-(1-R^2)y}{\tau\sigma}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-z_\alpha\sigma-(1-R^2)y}{\tau\sigma}\right), \qquad (2) an even function of yy that is strictly decreasing in |y||y| and tends to 00 as |y|→∞|y|\to\infty.

The proof is in Appendix A.

Integrating (2) over strata of YY (Table 2): for a predictor that explains half of the variance, the oracle covariate-conditional interval covers 70.5% of the top-10% outcomes and 37.5% of the top-1% outcomes, against 94.9% of the central 80%; with R2=0.9R^2=0.9 it covers 86.2% of the top decile. The shape of this profile is specific to the Gaussian model, so Table 2 also reports Monte Carlo values for heavy-tailed signals and skewed noise. With a Student-t3t_3 signal the top decile is still under-covered at R2=0.5R^2=0.5 (0.648), but the top 1% is covered at 0.625, because extreme outcomes then mostly come from extreme signals, which a covariate-conditional set follows. With right-skewed Gamma noise the oracle over-covers the lower decile (0.987) and covers only 0.418 of the top decile and 0.029 of the top 1%. In every case at least one tail stratum is covered well below 1−α1-\alpha. Tail under-coverage of standard conformal sets has been reported empirically (Wang et al. 2023; Boruah 2026a; Randahl et al. 2026); it persists for the oracle, so better covariate adaptivity cannot remove it. Coverage in rare strata requires calibration against the law of (X,Y)(X,Y) given Y∈BkY\in B_k, which is what stratified calibration does.

4. Proposed methods: stratified and relevance-weighted density-level conformal prediction

4.1 Stratified (Mondrian) calibration

Data are split into a proper training set 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} of size NN, a calibration set 𝒟cal={(Xi,Yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n and a test set. On 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} we fit a nonconformity score s:𝒳×ℝ→ℝ∪{+∞}s:\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} (small values = conforming) and choose the cut points, e.g. at quantiles of the training targets. Let k(y)k(y) be the stratum containing yy, Ik={i:Yi∈Bk}I_k=\{i:Y_i\in B_k\}, nk=|Ik|n_k=|I_k|, and, for levels αk∈(0,1)\alpha_k\in(0,1), q̂k=the rk-th smallest value of {s(Xi,Yi):i∈Ik},rk=⌈(nk+1)(1−αk)⌉,(3)\hat q_k=\text{the }r_k\text{-th smallest value of }\{s(X_i,Y_i):i\in I_k\},\qquad r_k=\lceil (n_k+1)(1-\alpha_k)\rceil, \qquad (3) with q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty if rk>nkr_k>n_k, which happens exactly when nk<1/αk−1n_k<1/\alpha_k-1 (i.e. nk≤8n_k\le 8 for αk=0.1\alpha_k=0.1). The stratified prediction set is Ĉ(x)={y∈ℝ:s(x,y)≤q̂k(y)}=⋃k=1K{y∈Bk:s(x,y)≤q̂k}.(4)\hat C(x)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}: s(x,y)\le \hat q_{k(y)}\}=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\{y\in B_k: s(x,y)\le\hat q_k\}. \qquad (4) The threshold applied to a candidate value yy is that of the stratum of that candidate, not of a prediction; this makes the guarantee stratum-wise. Equation (4) is an inductive Mondrian conformal predictor whose taxonomy assigns each example to the stratum of its label (Vovk et al. 2005; Vovk 2013); with the absolute-residual score it is BCCP (Randahl et al. 2026). When every sub-level set {y:s(x,y)≤q}\{y:s(x,y)\le q\} is an interval, as for residual or quantile scores, Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) is a union of at most KK intervals; density scores with a multimodal estimate can produce more pieces.

The following guarantee is the standard label-conditional Mondrian property (Vovk 2013), stated for outcome bins by Wang et al. (2023, Thm. 4.1) and Randahl et al. (2026). We restate it for an arbitrary score, with the edge cases used later (proof in Appendix A).

Theorem 1 (stratum-wise validity of Mondrian calibration). Suppose that, conditionally on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the points (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(Xn+1,Yn+1)(X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_n,Y_n),(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) are exchangeable, and let pk=P(Yn+1∈Bk|𝒟tr)p_k=P(Y_{n+1}\in B_k\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}). If the scores within stratum kk are almost surely distinct and finite, then also P{Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|Yn+1∈Bk,nk,𝒟tr}≤1−αk+1/(nk+1)P\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\, Y_{n+1}\in B_k,n_k,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\le 1-\alpha_k+1/(n_k+1). The levels αk\alpha_k may depend on nkn_k, and the score and strata may be any functions of 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}.

The guarantee holds for any score. For target shift between calibration and deployment, known facts specialise as follows.

Corollary 1 (target shift). Let 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} be i.i.d. from PP and let the test point be drawn from QQ, independently of 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} and 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Write Pk=P(⋅|Y∈Bk)P_k=P(\cdot\,|\, Y\in B_k) and Qk=Q(⋅|Y∈Bk)Q_k=Q(\cdot\,|\, Y\in B_k) for the within-stratum laws of the pair (X,Y)(X,Y) and πk=Q(Y∈Bk)\pi_k=Q(Y\in B_k); assume pk>0p_k>0 whenever πk>0\pi_k>0. (i) If Qk=PkQ_k=P_k for every kk with πk>0\pi_k>0 (the shift re-weights whole strata), then Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≥1−αkQ\{Y\in\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\ge 1-\alpha_k for every such kk, and Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)}≥1−∑kπkαkQ\{Y\in\hat C(X)\}\ge 1-\sum_k\pi_k\alpha_k whatever the πk\pi_k. (ii) For an arbitrary shift, Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≥1−αk−dTV(Qk,Pk)Q\{Y\in\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\ge 1-\alpha_k-d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k), where dTVd_{\operatorname{TV}} is the total-variation distance. (iii) Under label shift, Q(⋅|Y=y)=P(⋅|Y=y)Q(\cdot\,|\, Y=y)=P(\cdot\,|\, Y=y) with density ratio w=dQY/dPYw=dQ_Y/dP_Y; let mkm_k and MkM_k be the essential infimum and supremum of ww on BkB_k, 0<mk≤Mk<∞0<m_k\le M_k<\infty. Then Q{Y∉Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≤(Mk/mk)αkQ\{Y\notin\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\le(M_k/m_k)\,\alpha_k and dTV(Qk,Pk)≤tanh{log(Mk/mk)/4}d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k)\le\tanh\{\log(M_k/m_k)/4\}.

The proof is in Appendix A. Part (i) is the continuous-outcome form of the label-shift robustness of label-conditional coverage (Podkopaev and Ramdas 2021; Angelopoulos et al. 2024). For a continuous outcome, a label shift generally also changes the law of YY within a stratum, so exactness requires an unchanged joint law of (X,Y)(X,Y) inside each stratum. Part (ii) applies the coverage-gap bounds of Barber et al. (2023, sec. 4.5) within a stratum, and part (iii) follows from a bounded likelihood ratio. Both bounds are loose for the tilts of the target-shift experiment (Section 6.5), whose density ratios are unbounded on the open tail strata; they explain the direction of the effect, not its size. Marginally calibrated sets have no analogue of (i): their coverage under QQ is ∑kπkCovk\sum_k\pi_k\operatorname{Cov}_k, which can be as low as minkCovk\min_k\operatorname{Cov}_k. Stratified calibration needs no estimate of the shift, but it is exact only for shifts that act on the stratum probabilities.

4.2 The smallest sets with stratum-wise coverage

Theorem 1 leaves the score free; the score determines how large the sets are. For a prediction set CC let |C(x)||C(x)| be its Lebesgue measure and 𝔼|C(X)|=∫|C(x)|PX(dx)\mathbb{E}|C(X)|=\int|C(x)|\,P_X(dx) its expected size. By the Neyman–Pearson argument behind conformal density level sets (Lei et al. 2013), least-ambiguous classifiers (Sadinle et al. 2019) and covariate-indexed length-optimal sets (Kiyani et al. 2024), size-optimal sets are density level sets. The constraints in (1) are indexed by the label, so the problem separates by stratum and the thresholds are constant within each stratum.

Proposition 2 (size-optimal stratum-wise sets). Suppose the conditional law of YY given XX has a Lebesgue density f(y|x)f(y\,|\, x), that f(Y|X)>0f(Y\,|\, X)>0 almost surely, and that for each kk the random variable f(Y|X)f(Y\,|\, X) has a continuous distribution conditionally on Y∈BkY\in B_k. Fix α1,…,αK∈(0,1)\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K\in(0,1). Then there are thresholds tk>0t_k>0 with P{f(Y|X)≥tk|Y∈Bk}=1−αkP\{f(Y\,|\, X)\ge t_k\,|\, Y\in B_k\}=1-\alpha_k, and the set C⋆(x)=⋃k=1K{y∈Bk:f(y|x)≥tk}(6)C^\star(x)=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\{y\in B_k: f(y\,|\, x)\ge t_k\} \qquad (6) satisfies Covk(C⋆)=1−αk\operatorname{Cov}_k(C^\star)=1-\alpha_k for all kk. Every prediction set CC with Covk(C)≥1−αk\operatorname{Cov}_k(C)\ge 1-\alpha_k for all kk satisfies 𝔼|C(X)∩Bk|≥𝔼|C⋆(X)∩Bk|\mathbb{E}|C(X)\cap B_k|\ge\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)\cap B_k| for every kk, and hence 𝔼|C(X)|≥𝔼|C⋆(X)|\mathbb{E}|C(X)|\ge\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)|.

The proof (Appendix A) is the per-stratum Neyman–Pearson argument; it also covers data-dependent (e.g. conformal) sets whose stratum-wise coverage, averaged over the data, is at least 1−αk1-\alpha_k. With K=1K=1 it reduces to a single-threshold density level set, whereas HPD-split (Izbicki et al. 2022) uses an xx-specific threshold. Proposition 2 is an oracle statement. Stratified calibration of a uniformly consistent density estimate attains it asymptotically with fixed strata (Proposition 3, stated and proved in Appendix A, following the plug-in arguments of Lei et al. (2013) and Izbicki et al. (2022)).

Four consequences guide the method.

The optimal score is the conditional density, s(x,y)=−f(y|x)s(x,y)=-f(y\,|\, x), with stratum-specific thresholds; a single threshold is optimal only for marginal coverage.

The price of stratum-wise validity. Every set that meets the stratum constraints has marginal coverage at least 1−α‾1-\bar\alpha, α‾=∑kpkαk\bar\alpha=\sum_kp_k\alpha_k, so 𝔼|C⋆(X)|\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)| is at least the size of the optimal marginal set at that level, a single-threshold density level set. The two coincide if and only if t1=…=tKt_1=\dots=t_K. With a common level αk=α\alpha_k=\alpha the difference is the price, in size, of stratum-wise validity.

Coverage is reallocated across inputs. In a location–scale model f(y|x)=g{(y−μ(x))/σ(x)}/σ(x)f(y\,|\, x)=g\{(y-\mu(x))/\sigma(x)\}/\sigma(x) the optimal set is, in standardised units u=(y−μ(x))/σ(x)u=(y-\mu(x))/\sigma(x), {u:g(u)≥tkσ(x)}\{u: g(u)\ge t_k\sigma(x)\} within stratum kk. Its standardised width shrinks as σ(x)\sigma(x) grows, and it is empty when tkσ(x)>maxgt_k\sigma(x)>\max g: the oracle spends coverage where it is cheap. The stratified normalised residual (S-NCP), whose standardised width does not depend on xx, is optimal only for constant σ\sigma. The density score’s size advantage over S-NCP thus comes partly from the factor 1/σ(x)1/\sigma(x) and is paid for by lower coverage, and occasionally empty sets, for the noisiest inputs. S-NCP spreads coverage more evenly over the noisiest inputs and is preferable when coverage of high-noise inputs matters.

Shape and scope. Because thresholds differ across strata, C⋆(x)C^\star(x) need not be an interval even for unimodal f(⋅|x)f(\cdot\,|\, x). Optimality refers to size under the calibration covariate law; under a shifted QQ, C⋆C^\star stays valid in the sense of Corollary 1(i) but is no longer size-optimal. For targets with atoms (ties, zero inflation) Theorem 1 is unaffected, but a smooth density score is then valid without being size-optimal.

4.3 The SDLC procedure

Fig. 1 illustrates a prediction set and summarises the workflow of both methods.

SDLC instantiates (3)–(4) with the plug-in score s(x,y)=−f̂(y|x)s(x,y)=-\hat f(y\,|\, x), where f̂\hat f is estimated on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}; (5) holds for any f̂\hat f. We use the semiparametric location–scale estimator f̂(y|x)=1σ̂(x)ĝ(y−μ̂(x)σ̂(x)).(7)\hat f(y\,|\, x)=\frac{1}{\hat\sigma(x)}\,\hat g\!\left(\frac{y-\hat\mu(x)}{\hat\sigma(x)}\right). \qquad (7) Here μ̂\hat\mu is a gradient-boosted regression of YY on XX, and σ̂(x)=max{σ̃(x),𝜍}\hat\sigma(x)=\max\{\tilde\sigma(x),\varsigma\}, where σ̃\tilde\sigma is a gradient-boosted regression of the absolute out-of-fold residuals |Y−μ̂−j(X)||Y-\hat\mu_{-j}(X)| (three folds), the spread estimate of locally weighted conformal prediction (Lei et al. 2018). The floor 𝜍=max{10−3sd(Ytr),0.05median|Y−μ̂−j(X)|}\varsigma=\max\{10^{-3}\operatorname{sd}(Y_{\mathrm{tr}}),\,0.05\,\mathrm{median}|Y-\hat\mu_{-j}(X)|\} is shared by every method that uses σ̂\hat\sigma. The noise density is a defensive mixture ĝ=(1−λ)ĝKDE+λSt2(⋅/ŝIQR)/ŝIQR,λ=0.01,(8)\hat g=(1-\lambda)\,\hat g_{\mathrm{KDE}}+\lambda\,\mathrm{St}_2(\cdot/\hat s_{\mathrm{IQR}})/\hat s_{\mathrm{IQR}},\qquad \lambda=0.01, \qquad (8) of a Gaussian kernel density estimate (Silverman bandwidth) and the Student density with two degrees of freedom, St2\mathrm{St}_2, with robust scale ŝIQR=IQR/1.349\hat s_{\mathrm{IQR}}=\mathrm{IQR}/1.349. The mixture is fitted to cross-fitted standardised residuals: the out-of-fold residuals of fold jj are divided by a scale model trained on the other two folds, so that neither μ̂\hat\mu nor σ̂\hat\sigma has seen the residual it standardises (an in-sample scale fit shrinks the residuals, in our data by a median factor of 1.14 in standard deviation). This choice affects efficiency only, not validity, and was not tuned. The defensive component gives ĝ\hat g polynomial tails, so that far-out targets still receive a smooth, strictly decreasing density. The nonparametric ĝ\hat g captures skewness and heavy tails of the errors, and heteroscedasticity enters through σ̂\hat\sigma. If Y=μ(X)+σ(X)εY=\mu(X)+\sigma(X)\varepsilon with noise ε\varepsilon independent of XX, and λ\lambda and 𝜍\varsigma shrink to zero as NN grows, (7) can be uniformly consistent and Proposition 3 applies. Our implementation keeps λ=0.01\lambda=0.01 and the floor fixed and truncates to the domain 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D (Section 4.4), so Proposition 3 describes the limit of a sequence of such estimators, not the fixed-constant implementation itself. Otherwise SDLC targets the optimal sets of the best location–scale approximation, which affects size but never validity.

Three ablations replace ĝ\hat g by a standard normal density (SDLC-N, which isolates the factor 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x) only approximately), by a two-piece density with side-specific scales (SDLC-2p), or by a histogram density from a 40-class gradient-boosted classifier (SDLC-hist) (cf. Sesia and Romano 2021; Guha et al. 2024); their single-threshold counterparts are DLS-N, DLS-2p and DLS-hist (Supplementary Table S9).

4.4 Implementation

Strata. The primary stratification uses the training-target quantiles 0.10,0.25,0.75,0.900.10, 0.25, 0.75, 0.90 (K=5K=5: lower tail, lower shoulder, bulk, upper shoulder, upper tail). With tied targets, coinciding cut points are merged, so realised strata can differ from the nominal ones; the sensitivity analyses repeat the main comparisons on datasets whose realised tail strata are close to nominal.

Exact scores and the domain. Calibration scores are computed exactly at the observed target, Si=−f̂(Yi|Xi)S_i=-\hat f(Y_i\,|\, X_i). Sets are restricted to a bounded domain 𝒴D=[miny−0.05Δy,maxy+0.05Δy]\mathcal{Y}_D=[\min y-0.05\Delta_y,\max y+0.05\Delta_y] of the training targets (Δy\Delta_y the training range), intersected with [0,∞)[0,\infty) when all training targets are non-negative. A point with Y∉𝒴DY\notin\mathcal{Y}_D receives the score +∞+\infty, stays in its stratum, and counts as not covered. Membership of a test target is decided by the same exact rule, Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1}) iff s(Xn+1,Yn+1)≤q̂k(Yn+1)s(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})\le\hat q_{k(Y_{n+1})}, so the lower bound of Theorem 1 applies to the reported coverage, except that a test target outside 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D always counts as a miss. When q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty the reported set is Bk∩𝒴DB_k\cap\mathcal{Y}_D. We report the fraction of test targets outside 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D and how often q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty occurs.

Set geometry. Only the size, number of pieces, hull and tail alerts of a set are computed numerically. For a test point, Ĉ(x)∩Bk={μ̂(x)+σ̂(x)u:ĝ(u)≥−q̂kσ̂(x)}∩Bk\hat C(x)\cap B_k=\{\hat\mu(x)+\hat\sigma(x)u:\hat g(u)\ge-\hat q_k\hat\sigma(x)\}\cap B_k. We tabulate ĝ\hat g on a non-uniform standardised grid with analytic Student tails, interpolate linearly, and split every cell exactly at the stratum boundaries and the bounds of 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D. A four times finer grid changes mean set sizes by at most 0.2% and individual set sizes by at most 1.5% (Supplementary Section S3 and Supplementary Table S4). The same construction is used for every location–scale baseline (DLS, DCP, HPD-split, S-HPD, SDLC-N).

Algorithm 1. Stratified density-level conformal prediction (SDLC).

Input: proper training set 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}; calibration set 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}; stratum levels α1,…,αK\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K; stratum probabilities (e.g. 0.10,0.25,0.75,0.900.10,0.25,0.75,0.90). Output: prediction set Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) for any test input xx.

  1. Fit the mean model μ̂\hat\mu on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and compute three-fold out-of-fold residuals Y−μ̂−j(X)Y-\hat\mu_{-j}(X).
  2. Fit the scale model σ̃\tilde\sigma on all absolute out-of-fold residuals and three cross-fitted scale models; set σ̂=max{σ̃,𝜍}\hat\sigma=\max\{\tilde\sigma,\varsigma\}.
  3. Standardise the out-of-fold residuals with the cross-fitted scales and fit the noise density ĝ\hat g by Eq. (8); form f̂(y|x)\hat f(y\,|\, x) by Eq. (7).
  4. Compute the cut points from the training targets and define the strata B1,…,BKB_1,\dots,B_K and the domain 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D.
  5. for each (Xi,Yi)∈𝒟cal(X_i,Y_i)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} do Si←−f̂(Yi|Xi)S_i\leftarrow-\hat f(Y_i\,|\, X_i) if Yi∈𝒴DY_i\in\mathcal{Y}_D, else Si←+∞S_i\leftarrow+\infty; assign ii to stratum k(Yi)k(Y_i).
  6. for k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K do q̂k←\hat q_k\leftarrow the ⌈(nk+1)(1−αk)⌉\lceil (n_k+1)(1-\alpha_k)\rceil-th smallest score in stratum kk (Eq. 3; +∞+\infty if this rank exceeds nkn_k).
  7. return Ĉ(x)=⋃k{y∈Bk∩𝒴D:f̂(y|x)≥−q̂k}\hat C(x)=\bigcup_{k}\{y\in B_k\cap\mathcal{Y}_D:\hat f(y\,|\, x)\ge-\hat q_k\}, computed stratum-exactly on the standardised grid.

4.5 Computational complexity

Fitting (steps 1–3) requires eight gradient-boosted regressions: one mean model, three out-of-fold mean models, one scale model and three cross-fitted scale models. The kernel density estimate costs O(N+GglogGg)O(N+G_g\log G_g) by linear binning and FFT convolution on GgG_g grid points. Calibration (steps 5–6) costs O(nlogn)O(n\log n). Prediction (step 7) inverts the density level on each of the MM monotone runs of the piecewise-linear ĝ\hat g (typically a handful) within each of the KK strata, at O(KMlogGg)O(KM\log G_g) per test point, against O(K)O(K) for stratified interval methods such as S-NCP. One fit serves every α\alpha: changing α\alpha or the strata requires only recalibration.

RW-DLC (Section 4.7) has no comparable exact geometry, because its threshold q(y)q(y) in (10) depends on the candidate through ϕ(y)\phi(y). Its coverage is decided exactly at the observed target, but its sets are computed on a uniform grid of GG target values over 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D (G=4,000G=4{,}000 in the experiments): O(GlogGg)O(G\log G_g) per test point to interpolate ĝ\hat g and O(G)O(G) comparisons, with memory O(cG)O(cG) for a chunk of cc test points processed together. The relevance function adds set-up cost. With the exact Gaussian kernel density estimate used in our implementation, the floor pminp_{\min} costs O(N2)O(N^2), the calibration weights O(nN)O(nN) and ϕ\phi on the grid O(GN)O(GN); a binned estimate, as used for ĝ\hat g, would reduce this to O(N+GlogG)O(N+G\log G). The threshold qq on the grid is recomputed for each α\alpha or ϕ\phi at O(nlogn+Glogn)O(n\log n+G\log n), without refitting any model.

Deployment. SDLC and RW-DLC store eight gradient-boosted models, against five for S-NCP with an out-of-fold scale model, plus the tabulated ĝ\hat g and the thresholds (RW-DLC also the weighted calibration scores and qq on the grid). Changing α\alpha, the strata or ϕ\phi requires recalibration only; a change of the feature distribution requires refitting. Prediction is independent across test points and parallelises trivially. Wall-clock times are reported in Section 6.7.

4.6 Interval (hull) and floor variants

Hull variant (SDLC-hull). When an interval is required, the convex hull of Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) is reported. It inherits (5), but not the upper bound of Theorem 1 or the optimality of Proposition 2.

Floor variant (SDLC-floor). A user may want the efficiency of a single marginal threshold while protecting rare strata at a lower level 1−β1-\beta. The set Ĉfloor(x)={y:s(x,y)≤max(q̂αmarg,q̂k(y)(β))}\hat C_{\mathrm{floor}}(x)=\{y: s(x,y)\le\max(\hat q^{\mathrm{marg}}_\alpha,\hat q_{k(y)}(\beta))\}, with q̂αmarg\hat q^{\mathrm{marg}}_\alpha the ordinary split-conformal quantile at level α\alpha and q̂k(β)\hat q_k(\beta) the stratified quantile (3) at level β\beta, contains both the marginal set and the stratified set at level β\beta, so it has marginal coverage ≥1−α\ge 1-\alpha and stratum-wise coverage ≥1−β\ge 1-\beta in finite samples; we use β=2α\beta=2\alpha. This simple, conservative rule is not a contribution; level-optimising schemes (Wang et al. 2023; Kiyani et al. 2024) are principled alternatives.

4.7 Relevance-weighted coverage without strata: RW-DLC

Stratified calibration protects each stratum, but its protection ends at the resolution of the strata: outcomes in the top 1% lie inside the upper stratum BKB_K and are covered only on average with the rest of that stratum, and refining the strata quickly leaves too few calibration points per stratum. The imbalanced-regression literature describes the importance of outcomes not by strata but by a relevance function ϕ:ℝ→(0,∞)\phi:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty), for example the inverse of the target density (Torgo and Ribeiro 2007; Steininger et al. 2021). We therefore also consider relevance-weighted coverage Covϕ(C)=𝔼[ϕ(Y)𝟏{Y∈C(X)}]𝔼[ϕ(Y)],(9)\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\phi(Y)\,\mathbf{1}\{Y\in C(X)\}\big]}{\mathbb{E}[\phi(Y)]}, \qquad (9) which, for ϕ=1/pY\phi=1/p_Y, is coverage averaged uniformly over the range of the target, the continuous analogue of the macro-coverage that Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) study for long-tailed classification. A stratum-wise guarantee for every stratum implies (9) for every ϕ\phi that is constant on strata; (9) instead gives one averaged guarantee for a continuous relevance, without choosing strata.

Let ϕ\phi be fixed given 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, let Si=s(Xi,Yi)S_i=s(X_i,Y_i) be the calibration scores with weights ϕi=ϕ(Yi)\phi_i=\phi(Y_i) and W=∑iϕiW=\sum_i\phi_i, and define for a candidate yy q(y)=inf{θ:∑i=1nϕi𝟏{Si≤θ}≥(1−α)(W+ϕ(y))},Ĉϕ(x)={y:s(x,y)≤q(y)},(10)q(y)=\inf\Big\{\theta:\ \sum_{i=1}^n\phi_i\,\mathbf{1}\{S_i\le \theta\}\ \ge\ (1-\alpha)\big(W+\phi(y)\big)\Big\},\qquad \hat C_\phi(x)=\{y:\ s(x,y)\le q(y)\}, \qquad (10) with q(y)=+∞q(y)=+\infty when no such θ\theta exists. The candidate’s own weight sits at +∞+\infty, as in weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift (Tibshirani et al. 2019) and label shift (Podkopaev and Ramdas 2021).

Theorem 2 (relevance-weighted validity). If (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(X,Y)(X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_n,Y_n),(X,Y) are i.i.d. given 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and 0<𝔼ϕ(Y)<∞0<\mathbb{E}\phi(Y)<\infty, then 𝔼[Covϕ(Ĉϕ)]≥1−α\mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(\hat C_\phi)\big]\ge 1-\alpha, the expectation being over 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}. Equivalently, Ĉϕ\hat C_\phi has coverage at least 1−α1-\alpha for a test point drawn from the target-shifted law QQ with dQ/dP=ϕ(y)/𝔼ϕ(Y)dQ/dP=\phi(y)/\mathbb{E}\phi(Y).

The proof (Appendix A) applies the weighted-exchangeability argument of Tibshirani et al. (2019) with the likelihood ratio ϕ(y)/𝔼ϕ(Y)\phi(y)/\mathbb{E}\phi(Y), which depends only on the target. Two consequences matter in practice. First, (10) gives q(y)=+∞q(y)=+\infty exactly when ϕ(y)>αW/(1−α)\phi(y)>\alpha W/(1-\alpha): a candidate whose relevance exceeds the fraction α/(1−α)\alpha/(1-\alpha) of the total calibration relevance is always included. Rare targets are protected without strata, but only to the extent that the calibration set contains comparable relevance mass, which the Kish effective sample size W2/∑iϕi2W^2/\sum_i\phi_i^2 summarises. Second, Theorem 2 is also an exact guarantee under a target shift whose density ratio is proportional to ϕ\phi.

Proposition 4 (size-optimal relevance-weighted sets). Under the density assumption of Proposition 2, among all set-valued functions with Covϕ(C)≥1−α\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C)\ge1-\alpha, the expected Lebesgue size 𝔼|C(X)|\mathbb{E}|C(X)| is minimised by Cϕ⋆(x)={y:ϕ(y)f(y|x)≥t}C^\star_\phi(x)=\{y:\ \phi(y)f(y\,|\, x)\ge t\}, with tt chosen so that the constraint holds with equality (assuming the distribution of ϕ(Y)f(Y|X)\phi(Y)f(Y\,|\, X) has no atom at tt).

The proof is the Neyman–Pearson argument of Proposition 2 with the measure ϕ(y)f(y|x)dydPX\phi(y)f(y\,|\, x)\,dy\,dP_X in place of the stratum measure; its discrete counterpart for class-weighted coverage is given by Bhattacharyya et al. (2026). The proposition yields the score of relevance-weighted density-level conformal prediction (RW-DLC), s(x,y)=−ϕ(y)f̂(y|x)s(x,y)=-\phi(y)\hat f(y\,|\, x), calibrated by (10) and using the same density estimate (7) as SDLC. Relevance thus enters twice: it tilts the score towards relevant outcomes, which shapes the sets, and it weights the calibration, which delivers the guarantee. In the experiments ϕ\phi is fitted on the training targets only, ϕU(y)=1/max{p̂Y(y),pmin}\phi_U(y)=1/\max\{\hat p_Y(y),p_{\min}\} (“uniform over the target range”) or ϕH=ϕU1/2\phi_H=\phi_U^{1/2}, with p̂Y\hat p_Y a Gaussian kernel density estimate and the floor pmin=0.01maxip̂Y(Yi)p_{\min}=0.01\max_i\hat p_Y(Y_i) (Section 5). The suffixes -U and -H mark the relevance function: RW-DLC-U and RW-DLC-H are RW-DLC with ϕU\phi_U and ϕH\phi_H, and the ablations RW-DLS-U and RW-NCP-U use ϕU\phi_U.

5. Experimental design

The study answers seven research questions (RQ1–RQ7), reported in this order in Section 6. The datasets, seeds, splits, miscoverage levels, strata, base learners, methods and analyses of the main benchmark were fixed in a version-controlled configuration before it was run (Section 5.7).

  • RQ1 (tail coverage). Do marginal and covariate-adaptive methods under-cover rare target strata, and does stratified calibration restore stratum-wise coverage?
  • RQ2 (price). How much larger are the sets under stratum-wise validity, compared with marginal methods at the same and at a stricter level?
  • RQ3 (score). Does the density score of Proposition 2 give smaller stratified sets than other scores, and which component is responsible? We answer it with an ablation on real data, a synthetic study and a confirmatory replication.
  • RQ4 (relevance-weighted coverage). Does RW-DLC attain relevance-weighted coverage and cover the most extreme outcomes better than SDLC?
  • RQ5 (shift). How robust is stratum-wise coverage under target shift?
  • RQ6 (decisions). Are prediction sets useful for flagging extreme outcomes, compared with dedicated conformal tail classifiers and conformal selection?
  • RQ7 (sensitivity). How sensitive are the conclusions to the miscoverage level, strata, calibration-set size, density estimator, base learner, imbalance-aware training and grouped splits?

5.1 Datasets

The main benchmark uses the OpenML-CTR23 suite of 35 curated tabular regression datasets (Fischer et al. 2023); using a complete external suite avoids selecting datasets that favour the proposed method. By a pre-specified rule, we excluded the four datasets whose target takes fewer than 20 distinct values, because Lebesgue set size does not measure informativeness for such ordinal targets. The rule is a threshold on the number of distinct values only; count targets (e.g. abalone rings) and heavily discretised targets were retained. Targets with heavy ties or atoms are retained, such as the burned area of forest fires, which is zero for 47.8% of the fires. The remaining 31 datasets (Supplementary Table S1) have 517 to 72,000 observations and 5 to 971 features after one-hot encoding; 15 have a target skewness above 1 in absolute value.

Confirmatory datasets. For the replication, we took the regression datasets of the tabular benchmark of Grinsztajn et al. (2022) (OpenML suites 335 and 336), removed every dataset sharing source data with CTR23 and duplicate versions, and applied the same exclusion rule. This left 17 held-out datasets (Supplementary Table S2). As pre-specified, datasets with more than 50,000 rows were reduced to one fixed random subsample of 50,000 rows shared by all seeds; the CTR23 suite, whose largest dataset has 72,000 rows, was used as curated. Checks made after the analysis (Supplementary Tables S2, S3 and S17b) found that two held-out datasets (yprop_4_1, topo_2_1) contain the same observations and target, so the 17 datasets represent 16 independent targets; that six targets were log-transformed by the curators; that two targets are codes rather than quantities (visualizing_soil, seattlecrime6, the latter with 87% duplicate rows); and that the collection has at least 4,209 rows and no extremely skewed target (||skewness|≤|\le 6.7, against up to 59.0 in CTR23).

5.2 Splitting, leakage control and repetitions

Each of the 10 predefined seeds defines a random partition into proper training (50%), calibration (25%) and test (25%) sets; the replication uses five seeds. Every model, stratum boundary and density estimate uses the proper training set only. Several datasets contain repeated units, for example exact duplicate rows (9.1% of sarcos), repeated videos (video transcoding) and repeat sales (King County). The guarantees therefore refer to a new row from the same pool, not to a new unit (Supplementary Section S2 and Supplementary Table S3). Ten datasets were used during development or to diagnose the implementation (Section 5.7); the main comparisons are repeated without them.

5.3 Base learners

All methods share the same LightGBM models (Ke et al. 2017) with one fixed configuration (learning rate 0.05, 31 leaves, up to 2000 rounds with early stopping on a 10% internal validation split): a mean model, quantile models (for CQR), the scale models of Algorithm 1, and a multiclass model over 40 target bins (histogram density). No method receives specific tuning. The sensitivity analyses (RQ7) add a two-layer perceptron with the same pipeline and LightGBM trained with DenseWeight sample weights, which up-weight rare targets (Steininger et al. 2021).

5.4 Compared methods

Marginal or covariate-adaptive calibration. Split conformal prediction with absolute residuals (SCP) (Papadopoulos et al. 2002); normalised conformal prediction (NCP) (Lei et al. 2018); CQR (Romano et al. 2019); Mondrian conformal regression with five bins of the point prediction ŷ=μ̂(x)\hat y=\hat\mu(x) (Mondrian-ŷ) (cf. Boström and Johansson 2020; Boruah 2026a); DCP (Chernozhukov et al. 2021); HPD-split (Izbicki et al. 2022); and density level sets with a single threshold (DLS) (cf. Lei et al. 2013). DCP, HPD-split and DLS use the same location–scale density as SDLC, so the comparison isolates the calibration rule.

Stratified calibration. BCCP (Randahl et al. 2026), the absolute-residual score with stratum-wise thresholds, in union and hull form (BCCP-hull); the normalised residual with stratum-wise thresholds (S-NCP), in union and hull form; stratified CQR (S-CQR); the HPD score with stratum-wise thresholds (S-HPD); and SDLC with its hull and floor (β=2α\beta=2\alpha) variants. S-CQR omits the level optimisation of Wang et al. (2023) and is not an implementation of BFQR. S-NCP is the information-matched comparator of SDLC: both use the same μ̂\hat\mu and σ̂\hat\sigma.

Ablations. The chain BCCP → S-NCP → SDLC-N → SDLC adds, in turn, the scale σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x), the density weighting 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x) and the estimated noise shape. The histogram and two-piece densities are secondary results.

Tail-alert rules (RQ6). A set raises an upper-tail alert when it intersects the upper stratum BKB_K; for every method with stratum-wise coverage 1−α1-\alpha the alert recall is at least 1−α1-\alpha. We compare such alerts with a class-conditional conformal tail classifier that thresholds P̂(Y∈BK|x)\hat P(Y\in B_K\,|\, x) from the location–scale model (TC-LS) or the histogram model (TC-H) to guarantee recall 1−α1-\alpha; conformal selection with Benjamini–Hochberg control of the false discovery rate at qFDR∈{0.1,0.2}q_{\mathrm{FDR}}\in\{0.1,0.2\} (CS-BH-0.1, CS-BH-0.2) (Jin and Candès 2023); and the point-prediction rule (Point), “alert if μ̂(x)\hat\mu(x) is in BKB_K”. All methods are evaluated from the same cached model outputs with the exact rules of Section 4.4.

5.5 Evaluation metrics

For each test set we report:

  • marginal coverage and stratum-wise coverage (1) in each calibration stratum;
  • coverage in strata not used for calibration (training-target deciles, the top and bottom 5% and 1%) and in deciles of σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x), a diagnostic of covariate-conditional coverage;
  • mean set size divided by the training-target standard deviation (normalised size, also written size/sd(yy)), the share of empty sets and the number of disjoint pieces;
  • tail-alert recall, alert rate, precision, and the expected cost per unit when a missed extreme outcome costs cc times a false alert;
  • coverage under shift, by importance weighting of the test set: tilts ωγ(y)=exp(γζy)\omega_\gamma(y)=\exp(\gamma\zeta_y) (γ∈{1,2}\gamma\in\{1,2\}), with ζy=Φ−1{F̂Y(y)}\zeta_y=\Phi^{-1}\{\hat F_Y(y)\} the normal score of yy under the training distribution F̂Y\hat F_Y, and a positive control that multiplies the upper stratum by 5 and the lower by 0.5 without changing the within-stratum laws, so that Corollary 1(i) applies exactly. We report the Kish effective sample size of the weights.

Stratum coverages are averaged over seeds before taking the minimum across strata (“worst-stratum coverage”). Because the expected minimum of noisy estimates is at most the minimum of their expectations (Jensen’s inequality), worst-stratum coverage is biased downwards (cf. Boruah 2026b), we also report a null reference: the worst-stratum coverage expected under exact validity given the realised stratum sizes (Monte Carlo over the Beta–binomial law of split-conformal coverage).

5.6 Statistical analysis

Following Demšar (2006), the unit of analysis is the dataset: metrics are averaged over seeds and methods are compared across datasets. Set sizes are compared on the log scale by the geometric-mean ratio with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval, the Hodges–Lehmann estimate, wins and losses, and the sign test. Paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Holm’s correction within each family (Holm 1979). One-sided tests are used only for the hypothesis that stratified calibration improves worst-stratum and tail coverage over marginal methods; comparisons among stratified methods are two-sided. Equivalence of worst-stratum coverage is assessed by two one-sided Wilcoxon tests (TOST) with a margin of 0.01. Friedman mean ranks are descriptive only (Benavoli et al. 2016).

5.7 Protocol, deviations and confirmatory replication

What was pre-specified. We call an element of the analysis pre-specified if it was committed to version control before the corresponding evaluation was run; none was registered with a third party. The configuration of the main benchmark, the primary method and directional expectations for the research questions of the main benchmark (all except RQ4) were pre-specified in this sense.

What changed afterwards. (1) A loader bug that parsed string-typed features as missing was corrected and the affected datasets recomputed. (2) After the first run we learned of BCCP and BFQR; BCCP’s hull form, decile strata and tail-alert metrics were added. (3) The first implementation evaluated density-based sets on a coarse grid of the marginal target distribution, which inflated them; under it the size comparison with BCCP was not significant (Supplementary Section S5). (4) A review of the second run led to corrections applied to every method: cross-fitted standardisation, a defensive tt component instead of an ad hoc floor, half-open stratum pieces, a truncated domain and stratum-exact geometry. All reported results use the final implementation.

Consequences. Because the implementation changed after results had been seen, every size comparison on CTR23 (RQ3) is exploratory; the coverage results are unaffected in direction. To test the size comparisons, we committed a confirmatory analysis plan (hypotheses, tests, decision rules and script; Supplementary Section S6) to version control before evaluating any conformal method on the 17 held-out datasets; its commit identifier (ccba99b), commit time and the SHA-256 hash of the committed plan are listed in the anonymised code package (file PLAN_TIMESTAMPS.md); the version history itself will be made public upon acceptance. The time stamp is that of our repository, not of a third-party registry, so we call the plan pre-specified rather than pre-registered; base-model test metrics had already been computed on these datasets. Section 6.3.1 reports the outcome.

Relevance-weighted study (RQ4). RW-DLC was developed after the main benchmark had been run. Its analysis plan (relevance functions, comparators, metrics, hypotheses RW-1 to RW-4, tests and decision rules; Supplementary Section S7) was committed (identifier a9f31d2, listed in the same file) before RW-DLC was evaluated on any dataset, but after the SDLC results on the same held-out datasets, including its under-coverage of the top 1%, were known. RW-1 and RW-2 therefore test consequences of Theorem 2 and RW-3 an anticipated effect; only RW-4 could fail for empirical reasons, and it did (Section 6.3.1). RW-DLC, its ablations RW-DLS (score −f̂-\hat f) and RW-NCP (normalised residual), both with relevance-weighted calibration, and the comparators SCP, NCP, CQR, DLS (labelled DLS-M in the analysis plan), S-NCP and SDLC were evaluated with coverage decided exactly at the observed target and set sizes computed on a grid of 4,000 target values over 𝒴D\mathcal{Y}_D. Additional metrics are the relevance-weighted coverage (9), the mean and minimum coverage over training-target deciles, and coverage of the top and bottom 1%.

5.8 Use of a large language model

In line with the journal’s policy, we document that a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) was used as a research assistant in this study: to search and verify the literature, to write and test code, to orchestrate the computational experiments, to draft and edit the text, and to produce simulated adversarial reviews of the drafts. The model did not generate any data or result. Every number, table and figure in the paper is produced by the code provided as supplementary material from public data (Section 5.7), and every reference was checked against its publisher or index record. The authors checked the analyses and the text and take full responsibility for the content.

6.1 Marginal and covariate-adaptive methods under-cover the tails (RQ1)

All methods attained their nominal marginal coverage, but coverage of the target strata differed sharply. The seven marginal or covariate-adaptive methods covered 69.0%–82.0% of the targets in the upper stratum BKB_K and 44.5%–65.5% of the top 1%, and their worst-stratum coverage was 63.0%–78.3%. On 26–31 of the 31 datasets, it was below the range expected under exact validity. Marginal methods over-cover the central deciles and pay for it in the outer ones (Fig. 2); covariate adaptivity reduces the shortfall but does not remove it. Every stratified method, in contrast, covered 90.6%–90.9% of the upper stratum, with worst-stratum coverage 89.0%–89.3%, and was below the null range on at most 2 datasets, as expected under exact validity. SDLC’s worst-stratum coverage exceeded that of each marginal method on at least 29 of 31 datasets (one-sided Holm-adjusted p<0.001p<0.001; Hodges–Lehmann differences 0.081–0.250). The result is unchanged without the development datasets (p<0.001p<0.001) and for coverage of the upper stratum alone (p<0.001p<0.001). SDLC covered 86.8% of the top 5% and 73.6% of the top 1%, against at most 77.0% and 65.5% for the marginal methods; the top 1% is not calibrated, and its coverage stays below the nominal level for every method.

6.2 The price of stratum-wise validity (RQ2)

Stratum-wise validity enlarges the sets (Table 4). Holding the score fixed, stratified calibration increased the geometric-mean size by factors of 1.17 (normalised residual) to 1.27 (absolute residual). For SDLC relative to the single-threshold density level set (DLS) the factor was 1.24 (1.12–1.45), with a median of 1.11, for a gain in worst-stratum coverage of 0.231 (between 0.126 and 0.260 across scores). The price exceeded 1.5 on only 3 datasets for SDLC (Supplementary Section S8.7).

A fairer comparison is with marginal sets that buy tail coverage by lowering α\alpha (Table 5). At α=0.05\alpha=0.05 every marginal method still had a lower worst-stratum coverage (0.772–0.878) than SDLC at α=0.1\alpha=0.1 (0.891), and SDLC’s sets were smaller than theirs on 23–28 of the 31 datasets. Calibrating within strata thus gives more tail coverage for less size than raising the overall level.

6.3 Density, residual and quantile scores under stratified calibration (RQ3)

Among the stratified methods, which all had equivalent worst-stratum coverage (TOST with margin 0.01: p<0.001p<0.001 for every comparison with SDLC), SDLC produced the smallest sets (Table 6, Fig. 3). Its sets were smaller than those of BCCP on 24 of 31 datasets (geometric-mean ratio 0.902, 95% CI 0.841–0.956; Holm-adjusted pp < 0.001), than those of stratified CQR on 27 (ratio 0.795) and than those of S-HPD on 28 (ratio 0.947). Against the information-matched S-NCP, SDLC was smaller on 27 datasets (Holm pp < 0.001; Hodges–Lehmann ratio 0.962), but the gain was small and its geometric-mean ratio, 0.975 (0.941–1.020), was pulled towards one by a few datasets with large losses (Supplementary Section S8.7). The Hodges–Lehmann ratio, which describes the typical dataset, is our primary size estimand. Post hoc equivalence tests, seed-level reliability counts and the interval (hull) forms are reported in Supplementary Section S8.1.

SDLC remained smaller than all four stratified comparators without the development datasets, on the 26 datasets with near-nominal tail strata, at other α\alpha and with three or ten strata (Holm p≤p\le 0.002; Supplementary Table S5). Two subsets were less clear. On the 9 datasets with fewer than 1,600 observations no stratified score was consistently better (SDLC vs S-NCP: 5/4). On the 15 strongly skewed datasets, the advantage over S-NCP (12/3, Holm pp = 0.127) and S-CQR (pp = 0.127) was not significant.

Where the gain comes from (Table 6, Fig. 4). Adding the scale σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x) (BCCP → S-NCP) reduced size on average (ratio 0.926) but not consistently (18/13 datasets, pp = 0.111). Adding the factor 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x) (S-NCP → SDLC-N) reduced size on 26 of 31 datasets (pp < 0.001). Estimating the noise shape (SDLC-N → SDLC) added a smaller, less consistent reduction (ratio 0.993, 23/8, pp = 0.068). The two-piece density (SDLC-2p) did not improve on the symmetric one (normalised size 0.881 vs 0.874), and the histogram density (SDLC-hist) was far less efficient (normalised size 1.745; size ratio of SDLC to SDLC-hist in Table 6). The advantage over S-NCP is therefore mostly the coverage reallocation of Section 4 (Proposition 2 and its consequences): wider sets for low-noise inputs, narrower ones for high-noise inputs.

What the gain costs. The reallocation has the price the theory predicts. The worst coverage over deciles of σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x) was 0.769 for SDLC against 0.793 for S-NCP (Fig. 5). SDLC returned empty sets for 0.36% of test points (S-NCP 0.07%), concentrated on the noisiest inputs of high-R2R^2 datasets. SDLC also covered fewer of the most extreme outcomes than S-NCP and S-HPD: 0.736 of the top 1% against 0.789 and 0.790 (Holm pp = 0.031 and 0.017). It covered more than BCCP and S-CQR (0.687 and 0.698). The same held for the top 5%, where SDLC covered less than S-NCP on 22 of 31 datasets, and on the held-out data (13 of 17 datasets for the top 1%). Within the calibrated strata these differences cancel.

Synthetic designs. With known densities, the oracle SDLC set was smaller than the oracle normalised residual in all five designs (2.9% to 35.2%), and the estimated SDLC was smaller than S-NCP in 41 of 50 design-seed combinations (Supplementary Section S8.2).

6.3.1 Confirmatory replication on held-out datasets

On the 17 held-out datasets, analysed exactly as pre-specified (Supplementary Section S6), all four hypotheses were supported (Table 7).

  • C-H1 (tail coverage). SDLC’s worst-stratum coverage exceeded that of each of the seven marginal and covariate-adaptive methods (Holm pp < 0.001).
  • C-H2 (validity). Its worst-stratum coverage fell below the 5% quantile of the exact-validity null reference on 1 of 17 datasets (critical value 3).
  • C-H3 (set size). SDLC’s sets were smaller than those of BCCP (geometric-mean ratio 0.862, 14/3 datasets, Holm pp = 0.001), S-CQR (0.841, 15/2, pp < 0.001), S-NCP (0.977, 15/2, pp = 0.008) and S-HPD (0.984, 15/2, pp = 0.008). By the pre-specified rule (signed-rank test plus direction of the geometric-mean ratio), every comparison favours SDLC. The gains over S-NCP and S-HPD are small: the bootstrap intervals of their geometric-mean ratios (0.940–1.028 and 0.963–1.014) include one, although the reduction occurs on most datasets.
  • C-H4 (equivalence). The worst-stratum coverage of SDLC was equivalent to that of S-NCP and BCCP within 0.02 (TOST pp < 0.001 and < 0.001).

C-H1, C-H2 and C-H4 follow from Theorem 1 and check the implementation; only C-H3 could have failed for empirical reasons. The pre-specified secondary analyses were less favourable for the interval forms (SDLC-hull was not smaller than S-NCP-hull), and post hoc checks of the held-out collection (duplicate pair merged, continuous targets only, nominal tail strata) left every C-H3 decision unchanged; the advantage over S-NCP was confined to continuous targets and disappeared for strongly skewed ones (Supplementary Section S8.3, Table S17b).

6.4 Relevance-weighted coverage of the most extreme outcomes (RQ4)

Stratified calibration left the most extreme outcomes under-covered (top-1% coverage of SDLC 0.688 on the held-out datasets). RW-DLC was evaluated under its own pre-specified plan (Section 5.7); Table 8 reports the held-out datasets (17 datasets, 85 runs); Supplementary Table S18 lists the hypothesis tests. The plan also specified an exploratory arm on the 31 CTR23 datasets (Supplementary Table S19), reported after the held-out results below.

  • RW-1 (validity). The relevance-weighted coverage of RW-DLC was 0.898 on average, equivalent to the nominal 0.90 within the pre-specified margin of 0.02 (TOST pp < 0.001), as Theorem 2 predicts.
  • RW-2 (marginal methods miss the weighted target). RW-DLC exceeded every marginal method in relevance-weighted coverage, by 0.122 (NCP) to 0.180 (DLS) on average (Holm-adjusted p<0.001p<0.001 for all four comparisons).
  • RW-3 (extreme tail). RW-DLC covered 0.872 of the top 1% of outcomes, against 0.688 for SDLC (mean difference 0.184, 95% CI 0.063–0.310, higher on 13 of 15 datasets with top-1% test points, one-sided pp = 0.011). The definition-sensitivity of RW-3 is reported in Supplementary Section S8.3 (it held with the main-pipeline definition of the top 1%).
  • RW-4 (score). RW-DLC’s sets were smaller than those of the two ablations that use relevance-weighted calibration with an unweighted score, RW-DLS (geometric-mean ratio 0.885) and RW-NCP (0.904), but after Holm correction neither difference reached the pre-specified threshold (pp = 0.053 for both), so RW-4 was not supported.

On the CTR23 datasets all four hypotheses were supported: relevance-weighted coverage 0.901 (TOST pp < 0.001), top-1% coverage 0.907 against 0.715 for SDLC (higher on 28 of 28 datasets), and, unlike on the held-out data, smaller sets than RW-DLS and RW-NCP (ratios 0.828 and 0.874, Holm pp < 0.001).

The guarantee has a price elsewhere. Because RW-DLC averages coverage over the target range, it spends less on the bulk: its marginal coverage was 0.884 (minimum over datasets 0.750) and its worst coverage over target deciles was lower than that of SDLC (mean difference -0.080). Its sets were not reliably larger than SDLC’s (geometric-mean ratio 1.081, Hodges–Lehmann 1.113, median 1.174, 95% CI 0.916–1.240, descriptive). No test point had an infinite threshold; the smallest effective calibration sample size was 120 (median 1,368). The milder relevance ϕH\phi_H gave intermediate results. RW-DLC and SDLC thus answer different requirements: SDLC guarantees every stratum, and RW-DLC guarantees an average over the whole target range that reaches the outcomes beyond the strata (Fig. 6).

Dedicated tail strata (post hoc). RW-DLC’s advantage in RQ4 is over SDLC with the five primary strata, whose highest stratum is the top 10%. Stratified calibration can target the top 1% directly: with stratum edges at the training quantiles 0.01, 0.10, 0.25, 0.75, 0.90 and 0.99, the 1% strata received enough calibration points for a finite threshold on all but 1 held-out dataset, where the method returned the whole stratum in some seeds. Evaluated from the cached model outputs (Supplementary Table S17b), SDLC with these seven strata covered 0.906 of the top 1% (minimum over datasets 0.87), against 0.884 for RW-DLC, with a marginal coverage of 0.901 against 0.884; RW-DLC’s sets were not reliably smaller (geometric-mean ratio 0.952, Hodges–Lehmann 0.987, smaller on 9 of 17 datasets). On the smaller CTR23 datasets the picture changed. Dedicated strata again covered the top 1% as well as RW-DLC (0.913 against 0.917), but their 1% strata were often too sparse for a finite threshold (12 of 31 datasets), so that the method returned whole tail strata, and RW-DLC’s sets were smaller on 24 of 31 datasets (geometric-mean ratio 0.749, Holm pp < 0.001), at a lower marginal coverage (0.862 against 0.904). When a known extreme range has enough calibration points, a dedicated stratum delivers its coverage as well as relevance weighting; when it does not, RW-DLC reaches the same coverage of the extremes with much smaller sets, and it gives a guarantee averaged over the whole target range without a choice of strata.
