6.5 Target shift (RQ5)

Under the positive control, which re-weights whole strata, the stratum-wise coverage of every stratified method was unchanged, as Corollary 1(i) states, and their marginal coverage stayed at the nominal level (0.904 for SDLC), whereas that of the marginal methods fell to 0.838–0.877 (Fig. 7). Continuous tilts towards the upper tail also move mass within strata; under a strong tilt every method lost coverage of the upper stratum, the stratified ones less (0.770–0.833, against 0.550–0.726), and SDLC less than S-NCP (Supplementary Section S8.4).

6.6 Tail alerts and decisions (RQ6)

Every stratified method guarantees an upper-tail alert recall of at least 0.9; their mean recall was 0.978–0.988, and it was at least 0.9 on all 31 datasets (Supplementary Table S23). The price is a high alert rate. Among the stratified methods SDLC raised fewer alerts than BCCP (25/5 datasets) and S-CQR, but more than S-NCP (12/18). The dedicated tail classifier TC-LS attains the guaranteed recall almost exactly (mean 0.906) and raised fewer alerts than SDLC on every dataset (alert-rate ratio 1.559); for a pure yes/no decision it is the more efficient tool. Conformal selection (Jin and Candès 2023) controls the false discovery rate instead and flagged few units, with high precision (mean 0.766 at qFDR=0.2q_{\mathrm{FDR}}=0.2) but a mean recall of only 0.603; the point-prediction rule (Point) behaved similarly (recall 0.625).

The preferable rule depends on the cost cc of a miss relative to a false alert (Fig. 8; details in Supplementary Section S8.5). With equal costs, rules that raise few alerts (the point rule, conformal selection) were cheapest. At c=10c=10 SDLC’s expected cost did not differ significantly from that of TC-LS, and at c=20c=20 SDLC was cheaper on most datasets, because its recall exceeds the guaranteed 0.9; among the stratified scores, however, S-NCP gave the cheapest alerts.

6.7 Sensitivity analyses (RQ7)

Robustness. The conclusions held at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and 0.20.2, with three or ten strata, with a quarter of the calibration set (larger sets, because sparse tail strata then return the whole stratum), with a two-layer perceptron instead of gradient boosting, and with imbalance-aware DenseWeight training, which improved the tail coverage of marginal methods but did not remove the shortfall. Splits that keep repeated units together or hold out whole months changed little, but splitting video transcoding by video and Moneyball forward in time enlarged all sets several-fold and removed SDLC’s size advantage (SDLC larger than BCCP). The price of stratification rose with target skewness and fell with calibration-set size; SDLC was larger than S-NCP only on small or heavily tied datasets. Details are in Supplementary Section S8.6–S8.7 and Tables S5–S8 and S15. Computational cost. Measured like-for-like (same inputs, one thread, model predictions excluded; Supplementary Table S13), computing a prediction set took a median of 13.3 µs per test point for SDLC in batches, against 0.07 µs for S-NCP, a median factor of 207; including the model predictions, end-to-end prediction was only 1.32 times slower (median over datasets; at most 77 times, on a dataset with a very cheap point model). A single query outside a batch took about 6 ms (median over datasets; Supplementary Table S13), dominated by fixed per-call overhead. Calibration took at most 1.5 ms. RW-DLC, computed on a grid of 4,000 target values because its threshold depends on the candidate, cost 143 µs per test point, as much as SDLC on the same grid (ratio 1.01); fitting its relevance function took at most 4.9 s, its peak memory was at most 202 MB, and a finer grid changed mean set sizes by less than 0.1% (Supplementary Table S13). Both methods are therefore cheap next to model fitting, but an interval method remains preferable when single-query latency matters.

7. Discussion

7.1 Practical guidance

For practitioners who must report how often extreme outcomes are covered, we suggest the following.

  1. Decide which guarantee is required. Marginal coverage, however adaptive the score, does not protect rare targets, and lowering α\alpha is a less efficient substitute. If every target range must be covered at the nominal level, calibrate within strata (SDLC or S-NCP). If a known extreme range such as the top 1% matters most and each such stratum receives well over 1/α−11/\alpha-1 calibration points, give it its own stratum; this covered the top 1% at the nominal level on the large held-out datasets. If the extreme strata would be sparse, or coverage averaged over the whole target range is required without choosing strata, use RW-DLC with an inverse-density relevance: on the smaller CTR23 datasets it reached the same coverage of the top 1% with sets about a third smaller than dedicated strata, at the price of lower coverage in the bulk.
  2. Choose strata from training-target quantiles so that each stratum receives several times 1/α1/\alpha calibration points; otherwise use fewer strata or the floor variant.
  3. Use a score that includes the scale σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x). SDLC, S-NCP and S-HPD gave stratum-valid sets within a few percent of each other; SDLC was smallest on most datasets, while S-NCP is simpler, spreads coverage more evenly across noise levels, covers more of the extreme 1% and gives cheaper alerts. The residual score of BCCP and stratified CQR were clearly less efficient. When an interval is required, the hull of S-NCP was as small as the hull of SDLC on held-out data.
  4. Report hulls when an interval is mandatory. Stratified sets can be discontiguous: SDLC’s sets had 1.53 pieces on average (BCCP 1.47), mostly an isolated piece in a tail stratum whose threshold is lower than that of its neighbour (Supplementary Fig. S4). Such a piece says that an extreme outcome is plausible, but an interval is easier to communicate. SDLC-hull is valid and smaller than BCCP-hull, but loses part of the advantage.
  5. For yes/no decisions about extremes, match the rule to the costs. A class-conditional conformal tail classifier attains the same recall guarantee with fewer alerts and is the better choice when false alerts are expensive; among set-based alerts, S-NCP’s were the cheapest. Set-based alerts have higher recall, are cheaper when misses are very costly, and carry more information about the size of the outcome.

7.2 Limitations

Size cost and data requirements. Stratum-wise validity is paid for in set size, more so for skewed targets and small tail strata; with fewer than 1/αk−11/\alpha_k-1 calibration points the method returns the whole stratum. Pooling sparse strata (Ding et al. 2023), cross-fitted calibration (Barber et al. 2021a) and overlapping groups (Bairaktari et al. 2025) are natural remedies that we did not evaluate.

Granularity of the guarantee. The guarantee holds for the calibrated strata, not for arbitrary sub-ranges. Within a stratum, coverage is lower near its outer end (Remark A.1 in Appendix A), and shifts that move mass within a stratum reduce coverage (Supplementary Table S22); Corollary 1 explains the direction of this effect, but its bounds are loose for open tail strata. The guarantee is also marginal over XX within each stratum, so it says nothing about a particular input, and the density score deliberately trades coverage across inputs.

Density estimation and baselines. Proposition 2 is an oracle property, and Proposition 3 requires a uniformly consistent density estimate, which the location–scale model provides only when the noise shape does not depend on xx; flexible conditional density estimators may close the gap to the oracle. We did not stratify further covariate-adaptive methods such as conditional histograms (Sesia and Romano 2021) or localised conformal prediction (Hore and Barber 2025); they cannot beat the oracle density score, but their estimated versions may be competitive.

Evaluation scope. The benchmark covers tabular targets with at least 20 distinct values; the rule excluded ordinal targets with few levels, but count, heavily discretised, coded and time-indexed targets were retained (Section 5.1). The held-out replication covered datasets with 4,209 to 50,000 rows, six with curator-supplied log-scale targets and none with the extreme skewness of some CTR23 targets, so it does not test the regimes in which the CTR23 size advantage disappeared (small or strongly skewed targets). All splits are random splits of one pool: the guarantees and the efficiency results hold for new rows from the same pool, not for new units or future periods. Five held-out datasets are hourly or daily series, and under grouped splits coverage varied widely between calibration sets (for video transcoding, SDLC’s worst-stratum coverage ranged from 0.75 to 0.89 over seeds; Supplementary Table S15). All results use split calibration and one untuned base-learner configuration. The density-based implementation changed after earlier results had been seen (Section 5.7), which is why the CTR23 size comparisons are exploratory and were replicated on held-out data.

Applicability of the guarantee. Stratum-wise coverage requires exchangeability of calibration and test data, holds on average over calibration sets and over the test points of a stratum, and does not protect against covariate shift within strata.

8. Conclusion and future work

Prediction intervals that are valid on average can fail exactly where imbalanced regression needs them: on the rare outcomes. Even the oracle interval with exact covariate-conditional coverage under-covers the tails of the target, and on 31 benchmark datasets marginal and covariate-adaptive conformal methods covered only 63.0%–78.3% of the outcomes in their worst-covered stratum at a nominal 90%. We studied two guarantees that protect rare outcomes and the sets that meet them most efficiently.

Calibrating thresholds within strata of the target, an established technique known as Mondrian conformal prediction, guarantees coverage in every stratum for any score. For this guarantee, conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds are the smallest sets for the oracle, and SDLC, their plug-in version, gave smaller sets than bin-conditional conformal prediction with residual scores and than stratified quantile regression, on most CTR23 datasets and on 17 held-out datasets under a pre-specified analysis; the held-out collection contained neither small nor extremely skewed targets, and all splits were random splits of one pool. Among scores that use the estimated scale, however, the differences were within a few percent, and the simpler stratified normalised residual covered noisy inputs and the most extreme outcomes better. Strata also protect only at their own resolution. Relevance-weighted calibration avoids choosing strata: RW-DLC guarantees coverage averaged by an imbalanced-regression relevance function in finite samples, uses the score that is size-optimal for that guarantee, and in a second pre-specified study covered 88.4% of the top 1% of outcomes on held-out data, against 76.0% for SDLC with five strata, at a cost in coverage of the bulk. Dedicated 1% tail strata covered the top 1% as well, with sets of similar size on the large held-out datasets but about a third larger on the smaller CTR23 datasets, where such strata are sparse; RW-DLC is therefore the method of choice for sparse tails and for a guarantee over the whole target range. For yes/no decisions about extremes, dedicated conformal tail classifiers attain the same recall guarantee with fewer alerts.

Future work should combine the two guarantees, for example a relevance-weighted guarantee with a floor on every stratum; learn relevance functions or strata that minimise size subject to validity; replace the location–scale density by flexible conditional density estimators, whose gap to the oracle was largest under covariate-dependent multimodality; and extend both guarantees to grouped and dependent data, where our grouped and temporal splits showed that efficiency depends on transfer to unseen units and periods.

Sets. Fix xx and y∈Bky\in B_k. If yy lies in exactly one of Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) and C⋆(x)C^\star(x), then f̂(y|x)+q̂k\hat f(y\,|\, x)+\hat q_k and f(y|x)−tkf(y\,|\, x)-t_k have opposite signs (one is ≥0\ge0, the other <0<0), while they differ by at most ξN+δk\xi_N+\delta_k; hence |f(y|x)−tk|≤η:=ξN+maxkδk|f(y\,|\, x)-t_k|\le\eta:=\xi_N+\max_k\delta_k. Therefore 𝔼X|Ĉ(X)△C⋆(X)|≤∑k=1Khk(η),hk(η)=𝔼|{y∈Bk:|f(y|X)−tk|≤η}|.\mathbb{E}_X|\hat C(X)\triangle C^\star(X)|\le\sum_{k=1}^K h_k(\eta),\qquad h_k(\eta)=\mathbb{E}\,\big|\{y\in B_k:|f(y\,|\, X)-t_k|\le\eta\}\big|. For η<tk/2\eta<t_k/2 the set inside hkh_k lies in {y:f(y|X)≥tk/2}\{y:f(y\,|\, X)\ge t_k/2\}, whose measure is at most 2/tk2/t_k, and it decreases to {y∈Bk:f(y|X)=tk}\{y\in B_k:f(y\,|\, X)=t_k\} as η↓0\eta\downarrow0. By dominated convergence hk(η)→𝔼|{y∈Bk:f(y|X)=tk}|h_k(\eta)\to\mathbb{E}|\{y\in B_k:f(y\,|\, X)=t_k\}|, which is zero: continuity of the law of f(Y|X)f(Y\,|\, X) given Y∈BkY\in B_k gives 0=pk−1∬Bk𝟏{f(y|x)=tk}f(y|x)dyPX(dx)=pk−1tk𝔼|{y∈Bk:f(y|X)=tk}|0=p_k^{-1}\iint_{B_k}\mathbf{1}\{f(y\,|\, x)=t_k\}f(y\,|\, x)\,dy\,P_X(dx)=p_k^{-1}t_k\,\mathbb{E}|\{y\in B_k:f(y\,|\, X)=t_k\}|. Since η→0\eta\to0 in probability, (A.1) follows, and ||Ĉ|−|C⋆||≤|Ĉ△C⋆||\,|\hat C|-|C^\star|\,|\le|\hat C\triangle C^\star| gives the statement on expected size. ▫\square

Remark A.1 (within-stratum coverage profile). Under label shift, let κ(y)=P{y∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|Yn+1=y}\kappa(y)=P\{y\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\, Y_{n+1}=y\}, which is the same under PP and QQ. Then the change in stratum-wise coverage equals the within-stratum covariance 𝔼Pk[{κ(Y)−c0}{ℓk(Y)−1}]\mathbb{E}_{P_k}[\{\kappa(Y)-c_0\}\{\ell_k(Y)-1\}] for any constant c0c_0, with ℓk\ell_k the likelihood ratio of the proof of Corollary 1, so coverage is lost only if the shift moves mass within BkB_k towards values that are covered less often than the stratum average. For the oracle sets C⋆C^\star in the Gaussian model of Proposition 1, C⋆(x)∩Bk={y∈Bk:|y−x|≤ak}C^\star(x)\cap B_k=\{y\in B_k:|y-x|\le a_k\} for a stratum-specific radius aka_k, so the argument of Proposition 1 (with a=aka=a_k) shows that κ\kappa decreases in |y||y| within every stratum, that is, towards the outer end of a tail stratum; for the estimated sets the same pattern is observed empirically (Section 6.5). This is why a tilt towards more extreme outcomes can lower tail-stratum coverage even after stratified calibration.

Proof of Theorem 2. Write Zi=(Xi,Yi)Z_i=(X_i,Y_i) and let Zn+1=(X,Y)Z_{n+1}=(X,Y) be drawn from QQ with dQ/dP(z)=w(z)=ϕ(y)/𝔼ϕ(Y)dQ/dP(z)=w(z)=\phi(y)/\mathbb{E}\phi(Y), independently of Z1,…,Zn∼PZ_1,\ldots,Z_n\sim P; conditionally on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} the score ss and ϕ\phi are fixed. The joint law of (Z1,…,Zn+1)(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{n+1}) has density ∏i≤np(zi)⋅p(zn+1)w(zn+1)\prod_{i\le n}p(z_i)\cdot p(z_{n+1})w(z_{n+1}) with respect to the product of the dominating measures, so the vector is weighted exchangeable with weight functions (1,…,1,w)(1,\ldots,1,w) (Tibshirani et al. 2019, Lemma 3). Hence, conditionally on the multiset ℰ={z1,…,zn+1}\mathcal{E}=\{z_1,\ldots,z_{n+1}\} of observed values, P(Zn+1=zj|ℰ)=w(zj)/∑lw(zl)=ϕ(yj)/∑lϕ(yl)P(Z_{n+1}=z_j\,|\, \mathcal{E})=w(z_j)/\sum_lw(z_l)=\phi(y_j)/\sum_l\phi(y_l), and the test score Sn+1S_{n+1} is distributed as ∑jπ̃jδSj\sum_j\tilde\pi_j\delta_{S_j} with π̃j=ϕ(yj)/∑lϕ(yl)\tilde\pi_j=\phi(y_j)/\sum_l\phi(y_l). Therefore P{Sn+1≤Quant1−α(∑j≤n+1π̃jδSj)|ℰ}≥1−αP\{S_{n+1}\le \mathrm{Quant}_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{j\le n+1}\tilde\pi_j\delta_{S_j})\,|\, \mathcal{E}\}\ge1-\alpha, where Quant1−α\mathrm{Quant}_{1-\alpha} denotes the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of a distribution. Replacing the atom δSn+1\delta_{S_{n+1}} by δ+∞\delta_{+\infty} can only raise the quantile, and Sn+1≤Quant1−α(∑j≤n+1π̃jδSj)S_{n+1}\le \mathrm{Quant}_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{j\le n+1}\tilde\pi_j\delta_{S_j}) if and only if Sn+1≤Quant1−α(∑i≤nπ̃iδSi+π̃n+1δ+∞)S_{n+1}\le \mathrm{Quant}_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i\le n}\tilde\pi_i\delta_{S_i}+\tilde\pi_{n+1}\delta_{+\infty}) (Tibshirani et al. 2019, Lemma 1). The right-hand quantile equals q(Yn+1)q(Y_{n+1}) in (10), because the normalisation ∑lϕ(yl)=W+ϕ(Yn+1)\sum_l\phi(y_l)=W+\phi(Y_{n+1}) is the same. Taking expectations over ℰ\mathcal{E} gives Q{Y∈Ĉϕ(X)}≥1−αQ\{Y\in\hat C_\phi(X)\}\ge1-\alpha. Finally, for a fixed set CC, Q{Y∈C(X)}=𝔼P[w(Z)𝟏{Y∈C(X)}]=Covϕ(C)Q\{Y\in C(X)\}=\mathbb{E}_P[w(Z)\mathbf{1}\{Y\in C(X)\}]=\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C), so averaging over 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} yields 𝔼[Covϕ(Ĉϕ)]≥1−α\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(\hat C_\phi)]\ge1-\alpha. ▫\square

Proof of Proposition 4. Let CC satisfy Covϕ(C)≥1−α=Covϕ(Cϕ⋆)\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C)\ge1-\alpha=\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C^\star_\phi) and write h(x,y)=ϕ(y)f(y|x)h(x,y)=\phi(y)f(y\,|\, x). Pointwise, (𝟏{y∈Cϕ⋆(x)}−𝟏{y∈C(x)})(h(x,y)−t)≥0(\mathbf{1}\{y\in C^\star_\phi(x)\}-\mathbf{1}\{y\in C(x)\})(h(x,y)-t)\ge0, because the first factor is positive only where h≥th\ge t and negative only where h<th<t. Integrating over dydPX(x)dy\,dP_X(x) gives 𝔼[ϕ(Y)](Covϕ(Cϕ⋆)−Covϕ(C))≥t(𝔼|Cϕ⋆(X)|−𝔼|C(X)|)\mathbb{E}[\phi(Y)](\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C^\star_\phi)-\operatorname{Cov}_\phi(C))\ge t\,(\mathbb{E}|C^\star_\phi(X)|-\mathbb{E}|C(X)|). The left-hand side is at most zero and t>0t>0, so 𝔼|Cϕ⋆(X)|≤𝔼|C(X)|\mathbb{E}|C^\star_\phi(X)|\le\mathbb{E}|C(X)|. ▫\square

Statements and Declarations

Competing interests. The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

Funding. Funding information is given on the separate title page to preserve anonymity.

Author contributions. The contributions of each author are given on the separate title page to preserve anonymity.

Data availability. All datasets analysed in this study are publicly available on OpenML: study 353, the OpenML-CTR23 benchmark suite (Fischer et al. 2023), and, for the confirmatory replication, suites 335 and 336 (Grinsztajn et al. 2022). They are downloaded programmatically through the OpenML API by the provided scripts; the OpenML identifier and the licence recorded by OpenML of each dataset (“not stated” where OpenML records none) are listed in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2. The per-run result files released with the code contain target values of the calibration and test splits; for the two datasets whose licences restrict use (socmob: non-commercial scholarly and teaching use; health_insurance: GPL ≥ 2), these files are released under the same terms.

Code availability. All code, configuration files, raw per-run results, both pre-specified analysis plans and the analysis scripts are provided to reviewers as an anonymised code package (supplementary material), together with the commit identifiers, times and hashes of the analysis plans cited in Section 5.7; the code and its full version history will be deposited in a public repository upon acceptance. A single command (python run_all.py --mode full) regenerates every table, figure and number of the manuscript from the raw data. All experiments ran single-threaded per task on a four-core cloud machine (Intel Xeon, 2.1 GHz, no GPU). The logged task run times of the final pipeline sum to about 15 CPU-hours (about 4 hours wall-clock on four cores), and to about 26 CPU-hours including the superseded earlier implementations; energy use was not measured.

Ethics approval and consent. Not applicable. The study used only publicly available, de-identified benchmark data, including individual-level survey records (cps88wages, health_insurance) and crime reports (seattlecrime6); it involved no human participants or animals and no identifiable personal data.

Use of large language models. The use of a large language model in this work is documented in Section 5.8, as required by the journal’s policy.
